questions.stem:
The Headteacher of a school is thinking about making changes to the school day. She wants to take a sample of 60 students so that she can find out what the students think about the proposed changes.

The names of the 1200 students of the school are listed alphabetically.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Explain how the Headteacher could take a systematic sample of 60 students.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Number the 1200 students (1 – 1200) (Allow 0 – 1199).
B1: Use a random starting point between 1 and 20 (Must be between 1 and 20, allow 0 – 19).
B1: Select every $20^{th}$ person on the list.

parts.label: b(i)
parts.text:
(b) (i) Explain why systematic sampling is likely to be quicker than simple random sampling in this situation.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: They only need to generate one random number (a suitable comment).

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) With reference to this situation,
• explain why systematic sampling may introduce bias compared to simple random sampling
• give an example of the bias that may occur when using this alphabetical list
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: It is not random as the list is ordered alphabetically or not all combinations of sampling units are possible (a suitable comment).
A1: e.g. unlikely siblings would be selected (a suitable example).

parts.label: c
parts.text:
When the Headteacher completes the systematic sample of size 60 she finds that 6 students were to be selected from Year 9.

The Head of Mathematics suggests that a stratified sample of size 60 would be a more appropriate method.

There were 200 students in Year 9.

(c) Explain why this suggests that a stratified sample of size 60 may be better than the systematic sample taken by the Headteacher.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Number of Y9 students $= \frac{200}{1200}\times 60$ $[= 10]$ (a suitable calculation to find the number of Y9 students).
A1: The stratified sample gives a better proportion or is more representative oe (a correct explanation).

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Confidence interval for population mean (known variance)
parts.reason: Construction of confidence intervals is not mentioned anywhere in the statements; S5.3 covers hypothesis testing for a normal mean with known variance, not confidence interval construction. This topic is absent from the spec list entirely, so it is out even though it uses similar underlying normal theory.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Sample size calculation for confidence interval width
parts.reason: This depends on confidence interval theory from part (a), which is not covered by any statement; confidence intervals are absent from the spec.

parts.label: a
parts.reason: Spearman's rank correlation is not mentioned in any statement; S5.1 only discusses PMCC (r) and explicitly excludes calculation via formula, with no mention of rank correlation at all.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Hypothesis test for Spearman's rank correlation
parts.reason: Depends on part (a)'s Spearman's coefficient, and hypothesis testing using Spearman's rank correlation is not mentioned anywhere in the spec statements (only PMCC-based correlation testing appears in S5.1).

parts.label: (a)-(full)
parts.reason: The chi-squared test for association/independence, expected frequencies from contingency tables, and its critical values are not mentioned anywhere in the statements; S2.4 explicitly limits significance tests to those in Section 5 (binomial proportion, normal mean, correlation), which does not include chi-squared tests.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Unbiased estimators of population mean and variance from summary statistics
parts.reason: Although S2.3 covers calculating standard deviation from summary statistics for a single data set, the concept of an unbiased estimator (with n-1 denominator, sampling theory) for inferential purposes is not mentioned in any statement; this is inferential estimation theory absent from the spec.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Two-sample hypothesis test for difference of means
parts.reason: S5.3 only covers a hypothesis test for the mean of a single Normal distribution; a two-sample test for the difference of two means is not mentioned anywhere in the statements.

parts.label: c
parts.reason: S5.3 explicitly excludes knowledge of the Central Limit Theorem, and this part requires exactly that justification.

parts.label: d
parts.technique: Assumption for two-sample test (sample variance = population variance)
parts.reason: This is an assumption for the two-sample mean test which is itself out of spec (not covered anywhere), so this part is also out.

parts.label: a
parts.reason: question dropped: other parts out of spec

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Poisson probability calculation for expected frequencies
parts.reason: Poisson distribution is an explicitly named concept not mentioned in any statement, and per the exclusion rules a named concept absent from the statements makes the part out.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: Chi-squared goodness-of-fit test for Poisson model
parts.reason: Poisson distribution and chi-squared goodness-of-fit tests are not mentioned anywhere in the statements; S2.4 limits significance tests to those in Section 5, which excludes this test.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Probability involving linear combination of independent Normal random variables
parts.reason: S4.2 covers finding probabilities using the Normal distribution for a single variable, but the sum/combination of independent Normal random variables (with combined mean and variance) is not mentioned in any statement; this is a distinct technique absent from the spec.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Probability involving linear combination of Normal random variables (cost context)
parts.reason: Same as (a): linear combinations of independent Normal variables are not covered by S4.2 or any other statement.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: Mean and standard deviation of a linear transformation of a sum of Normal variables
parts.reason: This relies on the same uncovered linear-combination-of-Normals technique from (a)/(b), which is not mentioned in any statement.

parts.label: d
parts.technique: Solving inequality involving Normal probability for unknown parameter
parts.reason: Depends on the linear combination of Normal variables set up in (c), which is out of spec, and standard normal inverse used within that uncovered context.
